title: What is TF?
description: Coordinate frames, and how one sensor reading is placed in the world.

steps.title: Every part of the robot has its own frame
steps.body:
A **frame** is a coordinate system attached to something: the world, the robot's body, one sensor. The `/tf` topic says where each frame is relative to another.

The tree shows the chain here: `map` to `odom` to `base_link`, and then every sensor hangs off `base_link`: `lidar_link`, `laser`, `imu_link` and the camera.

steps.title: The robot moves; its sensors do not
steps.body:
Press play, or drag the timeline. Only one link in the tree changes over time: **`odom` to `base_link`**, the robot driving its figure-eight.

The LiDAR is bolted to the robot, so `base_link` to `lidar_link` never changes. That fixed offset is called an **extrinsic**.

steps.title: One reading, placed in the world
steps.body:
Each LiDAR sweep is published in the **`lidar_link`** frame: distances from the sensor, nothing more.

Look at the label at the top left of the 3D view. It says the cloud is shown as `lidar_link` to `map`. BAGEL multiplies the transforms along the path to put every point where it really was in the world.

steps.title: Choose which frame is the world
steps.body:
Open **Display** in the 3D view and look for the coordinate frame setting. With `map` as the world, the robot drives around. With `base_link`, the robot stays put and the world moves past it.

Neither is wrong. A fixed frame (`map`) is best for judging where things are; the robot frame is best for judging what the robot sees.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body:
If a sensor's extrinsic is wrong, its data lands in the wrong place and nothing lines up. A quick check: in the image view, pick `/lidar/points` as the LiDAR overlay. The dots should sit on the edges of the buildings and cars.

That is the same TF chain at work, from `lidar_link` to `camera_optical_link`.
